newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood forces fail to budge Taleban from pass.
newsitem.headline: Masood forces fail to budge Taleban from pass.

text.p: Commanders with ousted Afghan government forces said on Thursday an offensive launched the previous day had so far failed to budge Taleban troops from a strategic pass north of Kabul.
"We are in the same positions we were last night," one commander, Najim Khan, told reporters.
Led by Ahmad Shah Masood, military chief in the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, these forces are trying to dislodge the radical Islamic Taleban militia from the Afghan capital.
The Taleban took Kabul at the end of last month, giving them control of about two-thirds of the country.

On Wednesday, Masood's Jamiat fighters, along with troops and heavy weapons belonging to Uzbek leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, unleashed a large attack to grab the De Sabz pass, which commands the heights over Kabul, from Taleban forces.

The front was mostly quiet on Thursday except for some shells lobbed by the Taleban on to Masood's positions below another pass, Khair Khana, around 15 km (10 miles) north of Kabul, and a bombing raid on the village of Kalakan.
Lines of women, their faces covered in long blue or yellow veils, and their children fled Kalakan's narrow streets on foot.
"Why are they (Taleban) fighting women and children?" said Abdul Wahid, distraught after the bombing and leading his children out of the village.
Wahid's eight-year-old son, Mafur, was in shock after being slightly wounded in the head. Tears wet his dusty face while his siblings tensed to the crash of rockets falling on the next village.
A pile of cracked mud and timber was all that was left of one of three houses hit by the bombs. Men tried frantically to dig the bodies of four women out of the rubble.
"They were screaming before but now there is no sound," said Nurakhmad (one name), a neighbour helping to dig them out.
A reporter with the British Broadcasting Corporation who visited Kalakan later in the day, reported that 14 bodies, mostly of women and children, had been recovered.
A Taleban jet fighter also bombed the mountains around Jabal os-Siraj, a town 45 km (30 miles) north of Kabul and where Masood has his headquarters, around 11.30 a.m. (0700 GMT).
Jamiat fighters let off deafening blasts of anti-aircraft fire but to little effect as the Taleban plane flew high out of range.
"They are afraid," said one Jamiat fighter scornfully.
There has been heavy fighting north of Kabul during days of ceasefire talks being pressed by Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar and U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl.
Holl saw Dostum in his stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif on Wednesday and was due to fly to Kandahar, headquarters of the Taleban, for further talks on Thursday.
But his hopes of arranging a ceasefire were viewed as slim, with Dostum and Masood demanding the demilitarisation of Kabul. The Taleban have rejected this as unacceptable.
